sentences.text: Rhamphorhynchus is a genus of long-tailed pterosaurs named for its distinctive beak and snout.
Unlike many of its contemporaries, this animal possessed a long, rigid tail that ended in a diamond-shaped rudder supported by ligaments.
Its mouth contained twenty teeth in the upper jaw and fourteen in the lower jaw.
The smallest known individual of the genus had a wingspan of only 290 mm.
In contrast, the largest known specimen of the type species was estimated to have a wingspan of 1.8 meters.
The genus was formally described by Hermann von Meyer in 1846.
It was originally named Ornithocephalus muensteri because early scientists incorrectly believed that name was valid for Pterodactylus.
While fossils possibly belonging to the group have been found in England, Tanzania, and Spain, the best-preserved specimens come from the Solnhofen limestone in Bavaria, Germany.
A new species, R. etchesi, was named in 2015 based on wing remains from the Kimmeridge Clay in the United Kingdom.
This newer species is distinguished from others by a unique length ratio between its first and second wing phalanges.
Fossil evidence from stomach contents and coprolites confirms that the animal ate fish and cephalopods.
Adults developed a strong upward hook at the tip of the lower jaw.
Recent evidence suggests the creature likely foraged while swimming, aided by broad, large feet useful for propulsion.
One fossil specimen shows the jaws of a fish piercing the wing membrane of a Rhamphorhynchus.
A 2020 study supported the theory that the animal was precocial and could fly soon after hatching.
Researchers arrived at this figure by comparing the sizes of one-year-old specimens with two-year-old ones.
Comparisons of scleral rings suggest Rhamphorhynchus may have been nocturnal, similar to modern nocturnal seabirds.
Koh Ting-Pong and Peter Wellnhofer identified two distinct groups among adults differentiated by neck, wing, and hind limb proportions.
The type species of the genus is R. muensteri.
Phylogenetic analysis places R. muensteri in the family Rhamphorhynchidae as a sister taxon to Cacibupteryx and Nesodactylus.
Rhamphorhynchus lived during the Late Jurassic period, specifically the Tithonian age, in parts of Europe and Africa.
The animal lived from the Oxfordian to the Tithonian stages, between 159 and 143.1 million years ago.
It is debated whether Rhamphorhynchus had a crest; while Ferdinand Broili reported one in 1927, later examinations found no evidence of it.
Bennett suggested Rhamphorhynchus likely had an ectothermic metabolism, though he noted more studies were needed to confirm this.
Bennett found that specimens grouped into small-headed and large-headed sets, but concluded the case for sexual dimorphism was inconclusive due to a lack of morphological differences.
